answer.rationale: The decision hinges on whether memory_c2 actually licenses a wholesale primary switch under current conditions. I verify memory_c2 because it is the single most load-bearing memory for the switch option and the archived record should reveal the context it was earned in: what volume, whether the line had buffer, whether that vendor was ever primary at committed volume rather than a secondary or low-volume line. 'Onboarding was quick' at low stakes does not transfer to a line at 94% of committed volume with no buffer and 14 days to expiry. I verify memory_c4 second because negotiation is my intended path and I need to know whether the recovered margin came from genuine benchmarking leverage or from a one-time concession that will not repeat. Current intent: negotiate with the incumbent, explicitly benchmarked against the low-cost quote, which memory_c4 says moved them on both price and terms, while memory_c1 and memory_c6 indicate incumbent continuity has held across cycles and that term length is a real pricing lever. Kept as a small guarded commitment: short term, no multi-year lock, so a switch or a second source (memory_c3) remains open at the next review once the low-cost vendor is qualified without the line exposed. Uncertainty I am not resolving away: negotiation may not reach the full 18%, in which case the gap is real and I would rather surface a partial cut plus a qualification plan than buy the mandate with migration risk on an unbuffered line. Downstream risk flagged: an 18% cut pursued through price alone tends to be paid back in service scope, expedite rights, or allocation priority during a shortage, and none of the inherited memories record what was given up to obtain their cost wins. Also noting the memories are uniformly success stories with no failures recorded, which suggests a survivorship-biased archive rather than five independently validated tactics.
